analysis.one_liner: Taxes oil companies' 2022 windfall profits at 50% and rebates the money to taxpayers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, despite 48 House Democrats sponsoring or cosponsoring it.
analysis.plain_summary: During the 2022 spike in gas prices, this bill would have charged large crude oil producers a one-time 50% excise tax on profits above their pre-2022 normal levels, then sent the money collected back to most taxpayers as monthly energy rebates, phasing out for higher incomes. It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and never received a markup or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Most individual taxpayers would have received monthly energy price rebates during 2022, funded entirely by the tax on oil profits rather than by borrowing. The rebate is refundable (paid even to people who owe little or no income tax) and phases out at 5% of income above $75,000 for singles, $112,500 for heads of household, and $150,000 for joint filers, so lower- and middle-income households would get the full amount [S3]. Joint filers would get 150% of the individual amount [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers earning under the income caps

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 50% excise tax on the 'windfall profit' of crude oil producers that pump at least 300,000 barrels a day worldwide and had over $1 billion in gross receipts in 2005 — a definition that captures the largest integrated oil companies [S2][S3].
Windfall profit is defined as 2022 adjusted taxable income above the company's average 2015-2019 profit plus 10%, so only profits above the pre-spike baseline are taxed [S3].

All revenue collected would be paid back to eligible individuals as a monthly, refundable energy price rebate for 2022, with advance payments during the year modeled on the 2021 stimulus payment machinery [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large crude oil producers. The tax applies only to companies producing at least 300,000 barrels a day worldwide with more than $1 billion in 2005 gross receipts, and only on 2022 profits exceeding their inflated 2015-2019 average by more than 10%. Smaller producers, refiners, and other businesses would pay nothing. Consumers would pay nothing directly — the tax is on producers, and the revenue is returned to taxpayers rather than kept by the Treasury [S3].

drawbacks.text: Windfall profit taxes can discourage future investment in oil production. If companies expect a share of their profits to be taxed away during price spikes, they may drill or refine less, which over time can tighten supply and keep prices higher for consumers. The U.S. last tried a crude oil windfall profit tax in 1980 and repealed it partly for this reason.
The tax applies only to taxable year 2022 and the rebates expire after December 31, 2022, so it is a one-time measure that does nothing about energy costs in later years [S3].

The rebate phases out for individuals above $75,000 in adjusted gross income, so higher-earning workers hit by the same gas prices would receive little or nothing back even though they paid the same pump prices [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For lower- and middle-income households facing 2022 gas prices, the rebate would likely exceed the indirect cost of the tax, which is passed through prices only on future supply decisions. The main honest objections are economic: taxing windfall profits may reduce future drilling investment and does nothing permanent about energy prices, and the one-year design means the relief disappears with the tax.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, never received a markup or a floor vote, and died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Peter DeFazio introduced the bill on March 16, 2022 with 17 original cosponsors, during the spring 2022 spike in gasoline prices [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day, which is the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation [S1][S5].
The committee took no further action on the bill — no markup, no vote, no report — and it never reached the House floor before the 117th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest crude oil companies are better off: their 2022 windfall profits went untaxed and no revenue was redirected to taxpayers. Motorists received no rebate. The committee members who chose not to act avoided a vote that would have put oil taxation on the record in an election year.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big oil companies kept untaxed profits

for.name: Peter DeFazio
for.what_they_did: Introduced the windfall profits tax and rebate bill on March 16, 2022.

for.name: 47 of 213 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, making 48 House Democrats total behind it.

against.name: Richard Neal
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup; the committee record shows no action after referral.

against.name: American Petroleum Institute and major oil producers
against.role: Oil and gas industry trade association and the companies the tax would hit
against.what_they_did: Publicly opposed windfall profit tax proposals during the 2022 price spike, arguing they would discourage energy investment.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 47 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican support is recorded, and the Democratic-run Ways and Means Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would tax away 50% of their 2022 profits above their normal 2015-2019 level and hand the money to taxpayers. They opposed windfall taxes, which would have cost the largest companies billions.

industries.industry: Smaller oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: The tax's thresholds (300,000 barrels a day worldwide, $1 billion in 2005 receipts) exclude smaller producers and hit crude producers, not refiners, so competitors outside the tax's scope would gain relative advantage.

Monthly advance rebates and outreach requirements would create administrative work similar to the 2021 stimulus payments, which these firms help process; consumers would receive the payments directly.
